title: The Educated Barbarian: An introduction to Stoicism (Enchiridion analysis part 5)
summary: Fifth Enchiridion episode: shamelessly pursuing money makes you a worse citizen, a good citizen just does his own work well, Epictetus' lettuce example shows envy is silly because you did not pay the price, nobody deserves anything, keep a cold head about death whoever it strikes, and evil is a failure of good rather than its own nature.
claims: The goal of philosophy is to make you better for yourself and for others
Abusive pursuit of money makes you a worse citizen; most attacks on the very rich come from envy rather than a philosophical argument
Money only has value through the social contract; digital currency means something only because we agree it does
A good citizen does his own work well and takes care of himself, then family, friends and community, and by doing so helps the whole country
Nobody deserves anything; you get what you work for, and believing you deserve things breeds a victim mindset
Envy has no upside unless it pushes you to work; if someone has what you want, they paid the price and you did not
Wanting results without paying the price makes you insatiable and silly; effort and time cap how much anyone can accumulate
Even inherited wealth traces back to an ancestor who did the work; you can be that ancestor by getting to work now
Many people reason clearly about others' crises but lose their logic when they are the ones on fire
You cannot be stoic only two hours a day; the philosophy works only if applied all the time
Mourning is for yourself, for the absence of the person; knowing this helps the healing process
Evil has no nature of its own; it is a failure to fulfil good, so evil acts are perversions of your nature, not who you are
You are not evil for doing an evil thing; reject the act with confidence and do better in the future
